To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effects of naloxones on responding in monkeys are similar to the effects of nalxone on responding in humans.
morphine dependence in monkeys is maintained by fixed-ratio schedules and that the dose-effect functions for morphine and naloxone in escape and avoidance- escape procedures are similar.

(1) naloxone dose-dependently increases response rates during escape from continuous infusion of naloxone, but has little effect in an avoidance-escape procedure; (2) morphine dose-dependently decreases response rates in both escape and avoidance- escape procedures; and (3) morphine decreases response rates more in the absence of naloxone than in its presence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the behavioral effects of naloxones and the role of naloxone in drug abuse.
the effects of morphine on the acquisition of escape and avoidance- escape responding maintained by timeout from naloxone.
the development of behavioral procedures that will permit the assessment of the reinforcing and aversive properties of opioid antagonists.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the avoidance escape and escape procedures are not equivalent.
the rate of response in the avoidance-escape task is more stable than in the escape task.
morphine pretreatment produced dose-dependent decreases in responding, but that naloxone dose effects on responding were dependent on the behavioral history of each monkey.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the avoidance-escape schedule was more resistant to disruption by the substitution of saline for nalaxone, and that morphine pretreatment had a more profound effect on response rates during escape conditioning than in the avoidance-escape conditioning.
naloxone dose-response functions in the fixed-ratio escape procedure can be shifted by morphine pretreatment and that these shifts are not seen in the avoidance-escape paradigm.
the effects of naloxones on behavior are dependent on the behavioral history of an animal, the dose of naloxone, the dose and schedule of morphine, and the behavioral contingency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fixed-ratio escape and fixed-ratio avoidance-escape from an aversive drug are sensitive to the dose of the aversive drug and to pretreatment with a drug of abuse.
the avoidance-escape schedule can be used to study the behavioral effects of drugs in a manner that is similar to escape schedules, but with the advantage of a more gradual onset of the drug effects.
the behavioral consequences of naloxone depend on the behavioral context in which naloxone is administered.
